description: Search log and authority register for account-core contested questions C1, C2, C4, C10 and debt-collector status (milestone step A3). Every search is recorded, including those that found nothing.
citator: No paid citator (KeyCite/Shepard's) available. Later-history checks are open-web searches for citing cases; see each authority's later_history field.

searches.result: No relevant result; only unrelated federal circuit insurance bad-faith opinions. No appellate decision construing (h)(7) located.

No later appellate decision on bad-faith landlords' rights.

searches.query: AB 2801 (2023-2024) bill analysis list; Assembly Floor Analysis (concurrence, as amended Aug 23, 2024) retrieved by form POST
searches.result: Floor analysis confirms Senate amendments were chaptering-only (SB 611 conflicts), so the SJUD analysis of the Apr 25, 2024 version describes the enacted (h)(7). Saved. SJUD analysis (June 11, 2024) also saved: says (h)(7) 'does not require strict adherence; just a good faith attempt to comply' and that a good-faith violator may offset (citing 250 L.L.C. v. PhotoPoint, 131 Cal.App.4th 702, 727).

searches.query: Chaptered AB 2801 (Stats. 2024 ch. 280) text already saved at j1/lanes/enactments/sources/202320240AB2801.txt
searches.result: Legislative Counsel's Digest describes (h)(7) more broadly than its text: 'prohibit the landlord from making a claim against the tenant or the security if the landlord, in bad faith, fails to comply'. Enacted text: 'shall not be entitled to claim any amount of the security'. Section 1 intent: landlords not to subsidize improvements with deposits.

searches.query: "250 L.L.C. v. PhotoPoint Corp." 131 Cal.App.4th 702
searches.result: Located on Justia (original A105231 and modification A105231M), CaseMine, vLex, FindLaw, Leagle. Commercial lease under Civ 1950.7.

searches.query: Cases citing Granberry (cites=11612618167663359827) containing "bad faith", California courts, all 3 pages (23 results)
searches.result: No published decision addresses fn. 6 (rights of a bad-faith landlord) or construes 1950.5 bad faith. Relevant: 250 L.L.C. v. PhotoPoint (2005) discusses bad faith and setoff for 1950.7; unpublished (not citable): De Carlo v. Kosser (2013), Holsman v. Carrick (2010), Grabowiec v. Schopmeyer (2015), Sweeney v. Scully (2019). Others cite Granberry on setoff, statutory construction or unpassed bills (e.g., Fassberg (2007), Pacific Fertility Cases (2022), Coziahr v. Otay Water (2024)).

searches.result: Granberry (1995); Bauman v. Islay (1973) 30 Cal.App.3d 752; Granberry I (1984); People ex rel. Smith v. Parkmerced (1988) 198 Cal.App.3d 683; Runnymede Holdings v. No published decision defining bad faith for 1950.5 seen in snippets.

searches.query: "Peviani v. Arbors at California Oaks Property Owner" 62 Cal.App.5th 874 security deposit
searches.result: Located on Justia (E073950, 4th Dist. Div. 2, 2021); saved. Defendants were the owner LLC and its manager (JRK Residential). Court states elements of a 1950.5 wrongful-retention claim; bad faith is needed only for the statutory ('punitive') damages; reverses denial of class certification for the deposit class (reasonableness is the common liability issue).

searches.query: Granberry v. Islay Investments (Cal. Ct. App. 1993), FindLaw 1774861
searches.result: Retrieved (second attempt). Opinion approved a subjective bad-faith instruction: retention with the belief that it was not authorized by statute; negligence or honest mistake is not bad faith (CCP 128.5 analogy). Superseded by grant of review; not citable; Supreme Court fn. 4 left the instruction ruling unreviewed. Saved with caveat.

searches.query: "Runnymede Holdings" Foster 2023 96 Cal.App.5th Supp. 1 security deposit
searches.result: Located (App. Div. L.A., 2023). It concerns a mid-tenancy demand to increase the deposit and retaliation in an unlawful detainer, not move-out bad faith. Not relied on.

searches.query: "SM 10000 Property" Pecci 2026 Court of Appeal security deposit bad faith
searches.result: SM 10000 Property v. Pecci (B337813, 2d Dist. Div. 8, June 30, 2026) is unpublished (rule 8.1115) and decides only that a 1950.5 statutory-penalty claim raised first at trial was forfeited; applies former 1950.5; nothing on bad-faith meaning or (h)(7). searches.query: "Prudential Home Mortgage Co. v. Superior Court" 66 Cal.App.4th 1236 penalty one-year statute 340 section 2941
searches.result: Located (4th Dist., Div. 3, 1998). Saved from LawLink mirror. Holds the mandatory $300 forfeiture in Civ 2941(d) is a penalty under CCP 340(1); states the 'settled rule' that statutes giving damages additional to actual losses (double/treble) are penal; rejects MacManus v. A.E. Realty Partners.

searches.query: "Menefee v. Ostawari" 228 Cal.App.3d 239 one-year statute penalty
searches.result: Located (1st Dist., Div. 3, 1991), a landlord-tenant (SF rent ordinance treble damages) case. Saved from LawLink. Holds mandatory treble damages are a penalty (CCP 340(1)) but, following Holland v. Nelson, discretionary multiple damages are not.

searches.query: "Holland v. Nelson" 5 Cal.App.3d 308 treble damages discretionary statute of limitations 340
searches.result: Located (1st Dist., Div. 4, 1970). Saved from Justia. Discretionary treble damages under the Dance Act are not a penalty; CCP 338 (3 years) applies, partly because plaintiff could not otherwise know the period until the court exercised its discretion.

searches.result: Google sign-in wall; no result.

searches.query: "Holland v. Nelson" discretionary damages "section 338" penalty one-year "section 340" California Court of Appeal followed OR distinguished
searches.result: No later appellate treatment of Holland located by open search. One irrelevant unpublished 4th Dist. Div. 3 Labor Code penalty opinion (Taduran v. Glidewell, G064718, May 26, 2026) surfaced and was checked.

searches.query: "Holland v. Nelson" "penalty" "section 340" (later-history check)
searches.result: 8 results: Menefee (1991), Jensen v. BMW (1995) 35 Cal.App.4th 112, G.H.I.I. v. MTS (1983), Hypertouch v. ValueClick (2011) 192 Cal.App.4th 805, Warden v. Kahn (1979), Low v. Lan (2002) 96 Cal.App.4th 1371. Holland's mandatory/discretionary line followed in Menefee and Jensen and acknowledged in Hypertouch; no case found disapproving it.

searches.query: "Jensen v. BMW of North America" 35 Cal.App.4th 112 civil penalty "section 340"
searches.result: Saved (FindLaw mirror). Holds Song-Beverly's discretionary civil penalty of up to two times actual damages for willful violation is not a 340(1) penalty; it takes the underlying action's four-year period; '340(1) applies only where the penalty is mandatory'. Close analogue to 1950.5(m). Also surfaced: Shamsian v. ARCO (2003) restating the rule.

searches.query: "Hypertouch, Inc. v. ValueClick" 192 Cal.App.4th 805
searches.result: Saved (Justia, opinion on rehearing). Applies 340 to B&P 17529.5 liquidated damages because, once claimed and proven, some award is mandatory; discretion only over amount does not make a penalty discretionary (following TJX Companies (2008) 163 Cal.App.4th 80). Reaffirms Jensen/Holland for penalties the court may decline to award.

searches.query: Saved official FIN 100001, 100002 (jurisdictions/CA/texts/CA_FIN) and resolution_review/DEPENDENCY_AUDIT.md section 3
searches.result: DCLA 'debt collector' = regular debt collection for self or others, including composing collection letters; 'consumer debt' requires a consumer credit transaction; 100001(b)(1) exempts persons licensed under the Real Estate Law (BPC 10000 et seq.).

searches.query: DFPI PRO 05/21 debt collection licensing act rulemaking residential rent consumer credit transaction 2026
searches.result: DFPI DCLA regulations page; trade press; Assembly Banking analysis of SB 546 (2026) on a licensing exception.

searches.query: DFPI Debt Collection Licensing Act: Regulations, Opinions, and Releases (read 2026-10-03; curl blocked by Cloudflare, Nimble vx8 succeeded)
searches.result: Final DCLA regulations: PRO 02/20 (eff. Dec. 22, 2021) and PRO 01/23 (eff. July 1, 2025). PRO 05/21 (scope) remains a prefiling draft: third draft text released Oct. 24, 2025, comments closed Dec. 12, 2025; no formal notice or adoption listed.

searches.query: PRO 05/21 third draft text and invitation for comments (Oct. 24, 2025)
searches.result: Saved. Draft 10 CCR 1850.2(a)(1): 'Residential rental debt' is not consumer debt for the DCLA (COVID-19 rental debt exception struck in third draft, verified visually). Draft 1850.1: the 100001(b)(1) exemption covers listed entities and their employees only, not affiliates; DCLA exemptions do not exempt from Rosenthal. Draft, not law.

searches.query: SB 546 (2025-2026) Collection Licensing Act: exceptions: billing agents
searches.result: Amended in Assembly June 11, 2026; Assembly Appropriations do-pass Aug. 5, 2026; ordered to inactive file Aug. 17, 2026. Not enacted as of retrieval (the 2026 session's bill-passage deadline was Aug. 31). Bill text fetch failed on leginfo throttling (HTTP 500 / proxy reset).

searches.query: Assembly Banking and Finance analysis of SB 546 (hearing June 22, 2026)
searches.result: Saved. Committee staff: advance rent is not RFDCPA consumer credit, but utilities paid after usage are 'on credit' and subject to the RFDCPA (citing Davidson v. Seterus); the bill would exempt third-party 'billing agents' that calculate, allocate and deliver consolidated rent/utility statements for tenancies; staff notes the bill's sponsor (Conservice) is itself DCLA-licensed and that the bill implies such billing agents are currently licensees. Bill later moved to the inactive file (Aug. 17, 2026).

searches.query: Debt Collection Licensing Act opinion letter license required rent utility billing property management
searches.result: No DFPI opinion letter on rent, property managers or billing agents surfaced. Utilities' joint comment letters (2021, 2022) on PRO 05/21 argue billing incidental to core business is outside DCLA licensing, quoting the SB 908 Senate Banking analysis.

searches.query: PG&E/SCE/SoCalGas/SDG&E comment on PRO 05/21 (Oct. 5, 2021, posted 2022)
searches.result: Read (advocacy, not authority): cites Sen. Com. on Banking & Fin. Institutions analysis of SB 908 (Apr. 15, 2020 version) p. 8 for 'only persons and businesses who spend a considerable portion of their business collecting on credit debt ... persons who only incidentally engage in debt collection activities' excluded from licensure. Not saved; primary analysis retrieved instead.

searches.query: SB 908 (2019-2020) analyses list; Senate Banking and Financial Institutions analysis (analysisId 330841) retrieved by form POST; Assembly Banking analysis (Aug. 12, 2020) retrieved from abnk.assembly.ca.gov
searches.result: Both saved. Senate Banking analysis p. 6 quotes Senate Judiciary staff: licensing reaches 'only persons and businesses who spend a considerable portion of their business collecting on credit debt held by natural persons'; persons who 'only incidentally engage in debt collection activities' are excluded. Assembly analysis: DCLA uses the Rosenthal definitions; Real Estate Law licensees exempt.
